destinations.name: Mount Everest
destinations.short_description: Earth's highest peak, on the Nepal-China border in Solukhumbu, Koshi Province, and the focus of the Everest trekking and mountaineering region.
destinations.description:
Mount Everest, known in Nepal as Sagarmatha, is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level. It stands in the Mahalangur Himal range of the Himalayas, on the border between Nepal's Solukhumbu District in Koshi Province and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. Its height was most recently measured in 2020 through a joint survey by Nepalese and Chinese authorities as 8,848.86 m. The summit point itself is a border location rather than a visitor access point.

The mountain gives its name to the wider Everest region, a high-altitude landscape of glaciers, icefalls and deep valleys framed by peaks such as Lhotse and Cho Oyu. It was first climbed in 1953 by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, and it remains the central objective of Himalayan mountaineering. The region is also the homeland of Sherpa communities, whose villages, monasteries and mountaineering culture are part of the experience of travelling here, and the mountain sits within the UNESCO-listed Sagarmatha National Park.

Most visitors do not climb the mountain. They come to trek in the Khumbu, typically flying to Lukla and walking north through the Dudh Koshi valley and Sherpa settlements such as Namche Bazaar, with a long approach by road and trail from Jiri as an alternative. Treks lead to viewpoints and to Everest Base Camp, and the region combines high mountain scenery with a living Sherpa cultural landscape. Conditions, trail status and permits should be checked before travel.
destinations.access_info: Nepal Tourism Board describes the usual approach as a flight from Kathmandu to Lukla followed by trekking; a Jiri approach is also described. Check current flights, trail and permit requirements before travel.
data_quality_notes: Summit coordinate is a border point; independently verify the coordinate and the current district/province treatment before using for routing.
The 8,848 m figure on the UNESCO page reflects the older survey; the 2020 joint Nepal-China survey gives 8,848.86 m, which this description uses.
Summit coordinate is a border point, not a visitor access point; access context is described rather than a mapped entry.

destinations.name: Sagarmatha National Park
destinations.short_description: A UNESCO World Heritage national park in Solukhumbu, Koshi Province, protecting Everest, glaciers, deep valleys and Sherpa settlements.
destinations.description:
Sagarmatha National Park is a protected area in the Solu-Khumbu region of Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province, in eastern Nepal. It was gazetted in 1976 under Nepal's National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979. The property covers 124,400 hectares and spans an elevation range of about 6,000 m, from around 2,000 m up to the 8,848 m summit of Mount Sagarmatha, or Everest.

The park is an exceptional high-mountain area of dramatic peaks, glaciers and deeply cut valleys, encompassing the upper catchment of the Dudh Koshi River. Seven further peaks rise above 7,000 m. It is home to rare species including the snow leopard and the red panda, and its forests, grazing lands and river valleys support a distinctive Himalayan ecology. Most of the park lies above 5,000 m as barren high ground, with grazing land and a small proportion of forest below that.

What gives the park its particular character is that people live within it. More than 20 villages and several thousand Sherpa residents share the landscape with the protected wildlife, and their Tibetan Buddhist culture, monasteries and farming practices are recognised as part of the site's value. The park is the core of the Everest trekking region. Visitors walk through Sherpa settlements, past monasteries such as Tengboche, and along glacier-fed valleys toward base camp and viewpoints, with a buffer zone extending protection beyond the inscribed boundary.
destinations.access_info: Nepal Tourism Board lists a flight to Lukla or a bus to Jiri followed by trekking. Check current flights, trail and permit requirements before travel.
data_quality_notes: Best seasons reproduce NTB's March–May and October–November recommendation at broad season level; check current weather and park notices.

destinations.name: Everest Base Camp
destinations.short_description: The staging camp at the foot of Everest's climbing route in Nepal, reached on a multi-day trek through the Khumbu region.
destinations.description:
Everest Base Camp is the staging area at the foot of the climbing route on Everest's Nepalese, or south, side. There are two base camps on opposite sides of the mountain: the South Base Camp in Nepal, at an altitude of about 5,364 m, and the North Base Camp in Tibet, at about 5,150 m. The Nepalese camp lies in the Khumbu region of Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province, inside Sagarmatha National Park, at the head of the Dudh Koshi valley near the Khumbu Icefall.

It is not a settlement but a seasonal camp. During the spring climbing season it becomes a temporary village of tents used by expedition teams, guides and support staff, while in the trekking seasons it is a destination for walkers. The route to it follows a long-established trail through the Dudh Koshi valley, past Sherpa villages such as Namche Bazaar and Tengboche and through the national park, with high peaks, glaciers and icefalls along the way.

Most visitors reach the area by flying to Lukla and trekking north over roughly two weeks, with a longer approach from Jiri by road and trail as an alternative. The camp itself offers little view of the summit, so many trekkers continue to the nearby viewpoint of Kala Patthar for a closer look at Everest. Altitude is the central consideration on this route, and the trek is usually taken slowly with rest days for acclimatisation. Trail conditions and permits should be checked before travel.
destinations.access_info: Nepal Tourism Board says the commonly used trek starts and ends at Lukla, usually reached by air from Kathmandu. It also mentions a Jiri approach. The source describes a two-week trek; actual durations and access vary. Verify current flights, permits, altitude guidance and trail conditions.
data_quality_notes: No coordinate was added because an authoritative base-camp visitor point was not verified; do not substitute the Everest summit or a generic route point.

No coordinate assigned: an authoritative base-camp visitor point was not verified. Elevation (about 5,364 m for South Base Camp) comes from the Wikipedia 'Everest base camps' article; no official Nepali source was found that states it.

destinations.name: Gokyo Lakes
destinations.short_description: A group of high-altitude oligotrophic lakes in Sagarmatha National Park, Solukhumbu, designated a Ramsar wetland in 2007.
destinations.description:
The Gokyo Lakes are a group of high-altitude oligotrophic lakes in Sagarmatha National Park, in the Solukhumbu District of Koshi Province, eastern Nepal. They sit at an elevation of roughly 4,700 to 5,000 m and take their name from Gokyo Ri, the peak above them. In September 2007 the lakes and their associated wetlands, covering about 7,770 hectares, were designated a Ramsar site, and UNESCO lists the Gokyo and associated lakes among the Ramsar protections associated with the Sagarmatha World Heritage property.

Oligotrophic means the water is low in nutrients, which is typical of cold, high mountain lakes and gives them their clear, blue-green appearance. The lake system lies in the upper Dudh Koshi catchment in a landscape of glaciers, moraine and high peaks, with the Ngozumpa Glacier, one of the region's largest, close by. The lakes are among the highest freshwater lake systems of their kind, and the designation recognises their hydrological and ecological value within the national park.

Travellers reach Gokyo on a side route of the Everest trekking region, rather than on the main trail to Everest Base Camp. The walk climbs through Sherpa settlements along the Dudh Koshi valley and up to the lakes, where a small settlement of lodges stands beside the water. From the lakes, most visitors climb Gokyo Ri for wide views of Everest, Cho Oyu and the surrounding peaks, and some continue over the Cho La pass to link with the base camp route. The area is remote and high, so acclimatisation and current trail and permit information matter.
data_quality_notes: Coordinate is a mapped point for the lake group; verify which lake/access point it represents.

Ramsar designation details (September 2007, about 7,770 ha) are from the Wikipedia Gokyo Lakes article; the Ramsar Sites Information Service page could not be retrieved directly. UNESCO's Sagarmatha page confirms the high-altitude Gokyo Lake was declared a Ramsar site in 2007.
The record's coordinate is a mapped point for the lake group and does not identify a single lake or access point.

destinations.name: Kanchenjunga Conservation Area
destinations.short_description: A protected Himalayan area in Taplejung, Koshi Province, established in 1997 around the world's third-highest mountain.
destinations.description:
Kanchenjunga Conservation Area is a protected area in the Himalayas of eastern Nepal, in Taplejung District, Koshi Province. It was established in 1997 and covers about 2,035 square kilometres. It takes in the Nepalese side of Kangchenjunga, the third-highest mountain in the world, whose summit lies at 8,586 m on the border between Nepal and the Indian state of Sikkim, with its West and Kangbachen peaks falling inside Nepal's Taplejung District.

The conservation area lies in the far east of the country and adjoins protected land on both sides of the border: the Qomolangma National Nature Preserve in Tibet to the north and the Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim to the east, and it borders Sankhuwasabha District. It forms part of the wider Sacred Himalayan Landscape, a conservation approach that links protected areas across the eastern Himalaya. The area spans a great range of altitude, from subtropical valley floors to permanent snow and ice, and holds forests, alpine pasture, glaciers and high peaks.

The landscape is also a living one, home to communities including Limbu, Rai and Sherpa people whose villages, monasteries and farmland sit within and around the protected area. Trekking here follows remote routes toward the Kanchenjunga base camps, passing settlement, forest, pasture and glacier on the way, and the area is quieter and less developed than the Everest and Annapurna regions. The temple of Pathibhara Devi, reached from the town of Phungling, lies nearby and is often combined with a visit. Boundaries, entry points and current permit arrangements should be confirmed with the responsible authority before travel.
data_quality_notes: Verify boundary, entry points and current trekking/permit information with the responsible authority.

The Wikipedia article states the area 'comprises two peaks of Kanchenjunga'; that wording appears doubtful, so this description instead states that the West and Kangbachen peaks lie within Nepal, which is supported by the Kangchenjunga article.

destinations.name: Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve
destinations.short_description: A Ramsar-listed wetland reserve in the Koshi river floodplain of eastern Nepal, important for birds and wild water buffalo.
destinations.description:
Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve is a protected area in the Terai of eastern Nepal, covering about 176 square kilometres of wetlands in the floodplain of the Koshi River. It lies across the Sunsari, Saptari and Udayapur districts and ranges in elevation from about 75 to 81 m. It was established in 1976 and was designated a Ramsar site in December 1987, recognising the international importance of its wetlands. The reserve headquarters is at Kusaha.

The reserve is made up of extensive reed beds, freshwater marshes, grassland with patches of scrub and deciduous riverine forest, shaped by the shifting channels of the Koshi. It holds Nepal's last remaining population of the wild water buffalo, along with elephants, wild boar, hog deer, spotted deer, blue bull and jackal, and reptiles including the gharial crocodile; Gangetic dolphins are found in the Koshi River. Its birdlife is the reserve's other distinction: the Nepal Tourism Board lists 441 species, some of which migrate from as far as Siberia in winter, making the floodplain one of the country's foremost birdwatching areas.

A visit is centred on the wetlands and the river landscape. Activities are wildlife and birdwatching, typically on foot, by jeep or by boat along the river channels, with accommodation in resorts and tented camps near the reserve. The reserve is an easy add-on from Biratnagar, about a 90-minute drive away. The best seasons described by the Nepal Tourism Board run from October to March, alongside the hotter months of April to June and the rainy period from July to September, and current conditions should be checked before travel.

destinations.name: Ilam
destinations.short_description: A tea-growing hill district in Koshi Province, eastern Nepal, known for tea gardens, varied landscapes and cultural diversity.
destinations.description:
Ilam is a hill district in the far east of Nepal, in Koshi Province, with India's West Bengal to the east and Jhapa District to the south. The district covers about 1,703 square kilometres, and elevations within it range from roughly 140 m to 3,636 m above sea level, from lowland edges up to high ridge tops. Ilam town, also called Ilam Bazaar, is the district headquarters and is a quiet hill town in the Mahabharata range, acting as the base from which visitors explore the surrounding area.

The district is best known for tea. It is a major tea-producing part of Nepal, and much of the land is covered in tea bushes, with the tea industry growing and exports reaching markets in Europe and the United States. Alongside tea, the district's cash crops include cardamom, ginger, potato and broom grass, and the wider agricultural economy is diverse. Ilam is also described as one of Nepal's richest districts for cultural diversity and natural landscape, and it is called Charkhol, meaning area of four rivers, after the Jogmai, Puwamai, Mai and Deumai rivers that cross it.

A visit to Ilam is mostly about the landscape and the tea gardens. Walking through the tea estates, taking short hikes on gentle hills, picnicking in the gardens and visiting viewpoints are the typical activities, with Kanyam Tea Estate a well-known stop, and the Antu area associated with the Lepcha community, whose museum is being developed there. Mai Pokhari, a small lake with varied fish species, lies about an hour's drive from town, and Ilam Bazaar has hotels and a few tea-garden resorts that make it a base for day trips.

destinations.name: Pathibhara Devi Temple
destinations.short_description: A hilltop Shakti Peeth pilgrimage temple in Taplejung District, Koshi Province, reached by a climb from Phungling town.
destinations.description:
Pathibhara Devi Temple, also called Mukkumlung, is a Hindu temple on a hilltop in Taplejung District, Koshi Province, in the far east of Nepal. The temple stands at an elevation of about 3,794 m and is reached from the town of Phungling, the district headquarters, by a climb of several hours. It is one of Nepal's Shakti Peeth, sites associated with the goddess, and is among the country's significant pilgrimage destinations.

The temple is revered by more than one community. For Hindus it is a shrine to Pathibhara Devi, a form of the goddess, and it is believed that a pilgrimage here helps fulfil a devotee's wishes, which draws worshippers from across Nepal and from India. Long before the present temple, a large rock on the hilltop was revered by the Limbu people, who follow the Mundhum tradition and see the hill of Mukkumlung as a natural form of their goddess, Yuma Sammang. In 1995 a Pathibhara Area Development Committee was formed, and in 2001 the sacred rock was replaced with a statue of the goddess. Pilgrims offer prayer, animal sacrifice, and gold and silver.

The temple sits on a forested ridge with wide views over the Taplejung hills and toward the Kanchenjunga range, and the walk up from Phungling is itself part of the visit. The temple is a side route to the Kanchenjunga trek, so it is sometimes combined with longer walking in the conservation area. Festivals and pilgrimage seasons bring the largest gatherings to the hilltop, while at other times the site is quiet and the climb can be cold. Access routes and current pilgrimage arrangements should be checked locally.
data_quality_notes: Verify the mapped point, access route and current pilgrimage information with local/official sources.
Elevation of about 3,794 m is from the Wikipedia article and is not verified against an official Nepal source.

destinations.name: Halesi Mahadev Temple
destinations.short_description: A cave temple in Khotang District, Koshi Province, held sacred by Hindus, Buddhists and Kirat communities.
destinations.description:
Halesi Mahadev Temple, also known as the Halesi-Maratika Caves, is a cave temple beside the village of Mahadevasthan in Khotang District, Koshi Province, in eastern Nepal. The temple and cave lie between the Dudh Koshi and Sun Koshi rivers, at an elevation of roughly 945 to 1,440 m, about 185 km south-west of Mount Everest. The main cave is a natural formation reached by steps below the surface, with a large chamber and further passages.

The site is unusual in being sacred to three traditions at once, which is why it is sometimes called the Pashupatinath of the east. Hindus know it as the Halesi Mahadev Temple and associate the cave with Mahadeva, a form of Shiva, who is said to have hidden there from the demon Bhasmasur. Buddhists consider it the Maratika cave associated with the legend of Padmasambhava, who is said to have attained the long-life realisation here, and the caves are referred to in Himalayan literature as early as the 12th century. The Kirati Rai of the region worship Halesi as an ancestral deity, and their Mundhum oral tradition links an ancestor to the cave, so it is also regarded as an ancestral place.

The cave is approached as a pilgrimage, with worshippers climbing through forested hills to reach it and then descending into the cavern. Well-attended fairs and festivals are held here, notably around Shivaratri, Bala Chaturdashi and Rama Navami, when pilgrims gather from across the region and from India. Outside festival times the setting is quiet and rural. The temple is served by road, and access by jeep or motorcycle is possible; local conditions should be checked before travelling.

destinations.name: Janakpur
destinations.short_description: The capital of Madhesh Province and a Mithila pilgrimage city in Nepal's Terai, associated with Sita, temples, sacred ponds and Mithila art.
destinations.description:
Janakpur, also called Janakpurdham, is the capital city of Madhesh Province and lies in Dhanusha District in Nepal's Terai plains. It is a sub-metropolitan city and the main urban centre of the Maithili-speaking Mithila region. Accounts from ascetics, pandits and bards place the founding of the modern city in the early 18th century, and the ascetic Sannyasi Shurkishordas is regarded as the founder of modern Janakpur.

The city is named after King Janaka of the ancient Videha kingdom and is traditionally identified as the birthplace of Sita and the setting of her marriage to Rama, so it functions as a major Hindu pilgrimage centre. Janakpur is also a cultural hub: it is known for its temples, its sacred ponds, Mithila painting and a calendar of festivals, and the Maithili language is both the main first language and the lingua franca of the area.

A visit to Janakpur is largely a walking and temple-hopping experience. The principal landmark is the Janaki Mandir, and the city's other religious structures include the Ram Mandir, the Vivah Mandap and a series of historic tanks. Pilgrims come to bathe at the sacred ponds and to attend festivals such as Vivah Panchami, while visitors interested in living culture seek out Mithila artists and craft workshops in and around the city.
destinations.access_info: Nepal Tourism Board reports road travel from Kathmandu (about 390 km/10 hours), intercity buses from Gongabu and flights from Kathmandu of about 40 minutes. Durations are source estimates and should be checked against current services.

destinations.name: Janaki Mandir
destinations.short_description: A three-storey white temple dedicated to Sita in Janakpur, built in 1910 and the focus of the city's Vivah Panchami festival.
destinations.description:
Janaki Mandir is a Hindu temple in Janakpurdham, Dhanusha District, Madhesh Province, dedicated to the goddess Sita. It is a three-storey structure built of stone and marble, covering an area of about 1,480 square metres, and it is also known locally as Nau Lakha Mandir. The temple was completed in 1910, commissioned by Queen Vrisha Bhanu of Tikamgarh, and its construction cost is the origin of the nine-lakh name.

The temple is a principal pilgrimage site for the Mithila region and a major destination within it. Its walls carry Madhubani-style painting, and its rooms are decorated with coloured glass, engravings and lattice windows. The wedding mandapa attached to the complex is traditionally identified as the site of the marriage of Sita and Rama, and the temple is the main venue for the annual Vivah Panchami festival, which commemorates that marriage and draws large numbers of pilgrims. Janaki Mandir was added to Nepal's UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2008.

Visitors encounter a large, bright white building set among the busy streets of central Janakpur, with the mandapa and surrounding shrines forming a complex rather than a single hall. Visits are typically part of a wider circuit of Janakpur's temples and sacred ponds, and the atmosphere changes markedly during Vivah Panchami, when processions and rituals fill the area around the temple.

destinations.name: Ponds of Janakpur
destinations.short_description: A group of sacred historic tanks in Janakpur, with Ganga Sagar, Dhanusha Sagar and Parshuram Kunda held especially holy.
destinations.description:
The ponds of Janakpur are a group of historic tanks in and around Janakpurdham, Dhanusha District, Madhesh Province. The Mithila region is known for its many ponds, and the Nepal Tourism Board states that Janakpur is said to have as many as 72 ancient ponds of historical and mythological importance. They are a defining feature of the city's religious landscape rather than a single attraction.

Among the tanks, Ganga Sagar, Parshuram Kunda and Dhanusha Sagar are held especially sacred. Ganga Sagar is traditionally described as a pond that has never dried up, and is believed by devotees to hold water from the seven seas and from all sacred places. The ponds are closely tied to the wider Sita and Rama tradition of Janakpur, and ritual bathing in them is an established practice for Hindu pilgrims visiting the city.

For a visitor, the ponds are encountered as stepped tanks set among the streets, temples and ghats of Janakpur, usually combined with temple visits on foot or by short local trips. The typical experience is quiet observation of the tanks and their surroundings, watching pilgrims bathe and make offerings, and seeing how the water bodies structure the daily and festival life of the city.

destinations.name: Mithila Art
destinations.short_description: A traditional painting practice of the Mithila region, also called Madhubani art, made with natural pigments and passed down mainly by women.
destinations.description:
Mithila art, also widely known as Madhubani art, is a painting tradition practiced in the Mithila region of Nepal and India. It takes its alternative name from the Madhubani district of Bihar, India, which is where it originated and remains the most active centre of production. It is a living cultural practice rather than a fixed site, and in Nepal it is closely associated with Janakpur and the surrounding Mithila districts.

The painting was traditionally done by women and passed down within families from generation to generation. Artists work with fingers, twigs, brushes, nib-pens and matchsticks, and the paints are made using natural dyes and pigments, among them ochre and lampblack for reddish brown and black. The work is characterised by strong geometric patterns, and it carries ritual content for occasions such as birth and marriage and for festivals including Holi and Durga Puja. Traditionally the paintings were made on freshly plastered mud walls and floors of houses, and more recently on cloth, handmade paper and canvas.

For visitors, Mithila art is something encountered through the people who make it: in homes, workshops and community spaces, and in the walls and interiors of buildings such as the Janaki Mandir, which carries Madhubani-style painting. A visit usually involves watching or joining part of the painting process and learning how motifs drawn from nature, village life and religious stories are composed.
data_quality_notes: This is a cultural experience, not a single geocoded attraction; a specific community or workshop should be verified before publishing visitor details.

destinations.name: Gadhimai Temple
destinations.short_description: A Hindu temple of the goddess Gadhimai in Bara District, known internationally for the large animal-sacrifice festival held there.
destinations.description:
Gadhimai Temple is a Hindu temple of Gadhimai Devi, understood as an aspect of the goddess Kali, in Mahagadhimai Municipality in Bara District of south-central Nepal's Terai. The shrine sits in the central Terai plains near the Indian border, and the name Gadhimai is often used to refer to the festival held in the temple area as much as to the temple itself.

The temple is best known for the Gadhimai festival, a major Hindu festival held every five years. Reported traditions place its origins around 1759, linked to a local landholder's vow of a blood sacrifice. The event became known internationally for the large-scale sacrificial slaughter of animals, including water buffalo, goats, pigs, chickens and pigeons, and it has been estimated that 250,000 to 500,000 animals were sacrificed during the 2009 event. The practice has drawn sustained protest from animal-rights campaigners, and Nepal's Supreme Court ordered an end to live animal sacrifice in 2019.

A visit outside festival time is a low-key religious site visit in a rural Terai setting, with the temple as the focus of local devotion. During the festival period the area changes entirely, with very large numbers of pilgrims, temporary organisation of the site and the surrounding roads, and heavy involvement of local and cross-border traffic; conditions and any current arrangements should be checked with local sources before travelling.

destinations.name: Kathmandu Valley
destinations.short_description: A valley of seven UNESCO-listed monument zones that holds the densest concentration of Newar religious and palace architecture in Nepal.
destinations.description:
The Kathmandu Valley is the bowl-shaped basin in Bagmati Province that contains Nepal's capital, Kathmandu, along with the historic cities of Patan and Bhaktapur. Since 1979 UNESCO has protected the valley under a single World Heritage property composed of seven separate monument zones. The zones are the Durbar Squares of Hanuman Dhoka (Kathmandu), Patan and Bhaktapur, the Buddhist stupas of Swayambhu and Bauddhanath, and the Hindu temples of Pashupati and Changu Narayan. The government intervened in the definition of the listed area in 2006.

The valley's importance lies in the way its monuments form a living cultural landscape rather than an assembly of detached ruins. Temples, stupas, palace courtyards and traditional townhouses are still used for worship, festivals and daily life. The architecture in brick and carved timber, the metalwork and stone sculpture, and the essentially Newar character of the towns developed over many centuries and continued to be sustained by their communities. UNESCO placed the property on the List of World Heritage in Danger between 2003 and 2007 and in 2015 a major earthquake caused severe damage, much of which has since been repaired.

A visit to the valley is usually built from short trips between the monument zones rather than a single route. Most lie within a few kilometres of one another, and travellers commonly move between the Durbar Squares, the two great stupas and the river-side temple complex over several days. Between these formal sites the valley offers markets, alleys, courtyards and hilltop outlooks, and the wider basin can be viewed from its surrounding rims.
data_quality_notes: The mapped point is a valley-level representative coordinate, not a boundary or visitor entrance.

destinations.name: Kathmandu Durbar Square
destinations.short_description: The historic royal square of Kathmandu, known as Hanuman Dhoka, and one of the three Durbar Square monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley.
destinations.description:
Kathmandu Durbar Square, also called Hanuman Dhoka, is the historic royal square in the centre of Kathmandu Metropolitan City in Bagmati Province. It is one of the three Durbar Square monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property, alongside those of Patan and Bhaktapur. The square formed the seat of the Malla kings and later of the Shah dynasty until the court moved elsewhere in the nineteenth century.

The square is an open assembly of palace buildings, courtyards and temples in the Newar architectural traditions of brick, carved timber and stone. Among the best-known structures are the Hanuman Dhoka palace complex, the Taleju temple, the Kumari Ghar, which is the residence of the living goddess Kumari, and the Kasthamandap, a timber pavilion from which the city takes its name. The Kal Bhairav image and the nearby freestanding temples are part of the same dense ensemble, and the square remains an active setting for festivals and rituals.

Visitors generally approach the square on foot and spend time moving between the courtyards and the open fronts of the temples. The palace compounds contain museums, and the surrounding streets return visitors directly to the life of the old city. The 2015 earthquake damaged several structures in the square, and reconstruction has continued since. The square sits at the heart of the walkable historic core, so it can be combined with nearby markets and lanes in a single outing.

destinations.name: Patan Durbar Square
destinations.short_description: The palace square of Lalitpur, its Newar courtyards and temples forming one of the Kathmandu Valley's three Durbar Square monument zones.
destinations.description:
Patan Durbar Square stands in Lalitpur Metropolitan City in the district of Lalitpur, Bagmati Province, on the southern side of the Kathmandu Valley. It is one of the three Durbar Square monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property, together with Hanuman Dhoka in Kathmandu and the square at Bhaktapur. The square was the court of the Malla rulers of Patan.

The square and the old town around it contain some of the finest Newar architecture in the valley. The most celebrated building is the Krishna Mandir, a stone temple built in 1667, and the ensemble also includes the Bhimsen temple, the Vishwanath temple, the royal palace with its courtyards, and a bell and column added before the end of the seventeenth century. Patan is also known for its many Buddhist courtyards, called bahals, and for the surrounding craft quarters where metal casting, wood carving and stone work have long been practised.

Visitors typically explore the square itself and then walk into the adjoining streets of the old town, where the palace museums, temple platforms and neighbourhood courtyards follow one another closely. The square is small enough to cross on foot in minutes but detailed enough to occupy much longer, and it forms part of a wider historic area that can be seen over the course of a day.

destinations.name: Bhaktapur Durbar Square
destinations.short_description: The royal square of Bhaktapur, the easternmost of the three Durbar Square monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley.
destinations.description:
Bhaktapur Durbar Square lies in Bhaktapur Municipality in Bhaktapur District, Bagmati Province, in the eastern part of the Kathmandu Valley. It is the easternmost of the three Durbar Square monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property, alongside those of Kathmandu and Patan. The square was the palace complex of the Malla kings of Bhaktapur.

The square is known for a group of buildings from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The Golden Gate, or Sun Dhoka, dates from the mid-eighteenth century, and the adjoining Fifty-Five Window Palace, the Nyatapola temple with its stepped plinth, and the tall temple of Bhairav are among the structures that define the area. The monuments have survived repeated earthquakes, including those of 1833, 1934 and 2015, and reconstructions have followed each of them. The square forms the centre of a wider historic town whose brick lanes, squares and craft traditions are themselves part of the setting.

Visitors usually enter the old town on foot and spend several hours among the palace courtyards, temples and open squares. Pottery, weaving and other traditional crafts can be seen in the surrounding quarters, and the town's layout allows a walk to continue well beyond the monument zone itself. Because the square sits within the living town, its temples and public spaces remain in active everyday use.

destinations.name: Swayambhunath
destinations.short_description: A hilltop stupa and religious ensemble above Kathmandu, venerated by both Buddhists and Hindus and a Kathmandu Valley monument zone.
destinations.description:
Swayambhunath is a religious complex centred on a stupa on a hill to the west of central Kathmandu, in Kathmandu Metropolitan City, Bagmati Province. It is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property. The site is venerated by Buddhists and also treated as sacred by Hindus, and its hilltop position gives it a distinct setting above the city.

The complex is built around a domed stupa crowned by a gilded spire painted with the eyes of the Buddha, and it is surrounded by smaller shrines, chaityas, prayer wheels and monastic and temple buildings. Swayambhunath has long been a place of pilgrimage and is associated with the foundation legends of the valley. The site shows the close overlap of Buddhist and Hindu practice in Nepal, and it continues to be the focus of festivals and everyday worship as much as of heritage interest.

Visitors reach the complex by a long stairway of stone steps that climbs the hill, or by a road that arrives nearer the top. Once there, they move around the stupa in the customary clockwise direction, past the shrine buildings and smaller monuments, with views across Kathmandu in several directions. The site is commonly combined with nearby parts of the city in a half-day visit, and the walk up and down is part of the experience for many travellers.

destinations.name: Boudhanath Stupa
destinations.short_description: A vast white stupa in eastern Kathmandu, described by UNESCO as the largest in Nepal, and one of the Kathmandu Valley monument zones.
destinations.description:
Boudhanath Stupa stands in Kathmandu Metropolitan City, Bagmati Province, in the eastern part of the city. It is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property, and UNESCO describes it as the largest stupa in Nepal. The surrounding neighbourhood is a centre of Tibetan Buddhist life in Kathmandu.

The stupa's form is a large whitewashed dome rising to a square painted harmika and a gilded spire, encircled by a low wall set with prayer wheels. It is a major pilgrimage destination and is closely associated with Tibetan Buddhism, having become a focus for Tibetan communities and monasteries in Nepal. The stupa and its setting continue to function as a place of daily worship, with circumambulation, offerings and festivals forming part of its regular life rather than a scheduled attraction.

Visitors usually walk around the base of the stupa in the clockwise direction along the encircling path, alongside pilgrims turning the prayer wheels. The rooftops and terraces of the surrounding buildings give elevated views of the dome, and the lanes around the stupa contain monasteries, shops and small restaurants. A visit is typically quiet and unhurried, lasting somewhere between a short walk and a longer stay in the neighbourhood.

destinations.name: Pashupatinath Temple
destinations.short_description: An extensive Hindu temple precinct on the Bagmati river in Kathmandu and one of the Kathmandu Valley's seven monument zones.
destinations.description:
Pashupatinath is a Hindu temple precinct on the banks of the Bagmati river in Kathmandu Metropolitan City, Bagmati Province. UNESCO describes it as an extensive temple precinct and includes it as one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property. The complex covers a large area of temples, shrines, platforms and river-side structures rather than a single building.

The principal temple is dedicated to Shiva as Pashupati, and the site is one of the most important Hindu pilgrimage destinations in Nepal. The precinct contains many temples and shrines, and the Bagmati river flows through it, with stone platforms and ghats along the banks used for ritual bathing and for cremation rites. The complex is the focus of major festivals, above all Maha Shivaratri, when large numbers of pilgrims gather. Because it remains an active religious site, much of the precinct is given over to worship rather than to display.

Visitors move through the complex on foot along paths and terraces, passing temple courtyards, the river and the surrounding wooded ground. Views of the main temple are available from across the river, and the wider precinct can be explored over an hour or more. The atmosphere varies greatly between ordinary days and festival times, when crowds fill the site and the surrounding routes.

destinations.name: Changu Narayan Temple
destinations.short_description: A hilltop Hindu temple complex near Bhaktapur with an early fifth-century inscription, one of the Kathmandu Valley monument zones.
destinations.description:
Changu Narayan is a Hindu temple complex in Changunarayan Municipality, Bhaktapur District, Bagmati Province, on a ridge to the north of Bhaktapur. It is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property. UNESCO describes it as a temple complex set within a traditional Newar settlement and notes an inscription from the early fifth century.

The temple is dedicated to Vishnu in his form as Narayan, and the site is considered one of the oldest Hindu temple locations in the Kathmandu Valley. Its stone pillar carries an inscription associated with the Licchavi king Manadeva and dated to the fifth century, and the complex includes stone sculptures, carved struts and other decorative and devotional elements from different periods. Around the temple, the traditional settlement shows the pattern of Newar village building in brick and timber, and the temple remains in active worship.

Visitors reach the complex along the ridge road or on foot, arriving at an open court facing the temple and its pillar. The site is compact but richly detailed, and the walk through the adjoining village streets rounds out a visit. There are open views along the ridge towards the valley, and the temple is often seen on the same trip as Bhaktapur, a short distance to the south.

destinations.name: Langtang National Park
destinations.short_description: Nepal's first Himalayan national park, a protected area of high mountains, forests and alpine valleys north of Kathmandu in Bagmati Province.
destinations.description:
Langtang National Park is a protected area in the central Nepal Himalaya, within Bagmati Province and extending across the districts of Nuwakot, Rasuwa and Sindhupalchok. It was established in 1976 as the country's first Himalayan national park and covers an area of about 1,710 square kilometres, with a buffer zone added in 1998. The park lies north of Kathmandu, close to the border with the Tibet region of China.

The park spans a wide range of altitude and habitat, from subtropical forest through temperate and subalpine woodland to high alpine country and permanent snow, which gives it considerable biological and landscape variety. It contains glaciers, river valleys, high pastures and peaks, and it is home to wildlife including red panda, Himalayan black bear, langur and various birds, along with populations of snow leopard and musk deer in its higher reaches. Several settlements and herding areas lie within and beside the park, and the valleys have long been used by local communities and by herders moving with livestock to summer pastures.

The park is best known as the setting of the Langtang trek, which follows the Langtang valley northwards through villages and forests towards the head of the valley and its viewpoints, with side routes to high lakes and passes. The trekking season normally runs in the drier months of spring and autumn, when the trails and high routes are most accessible. Visits generally take the form of multi-day walks between settlements, with tea houses providing accommodation, and the landscapes range from terraced lower valleys to open alpine ground beneath the peaks.

destinations.name: Gosaikunda Lake
destinations.short_description: A high alpine lake in Rasuwa District held sacred by Hindus and a focus of pilgrimage and trekking in the Langtang region.
destinations.description:
Gosaikunda is a high alpine lake in Rasuwa District, Bagmati Province, in the Langtang region north of Kathmandu. It lies in the upper Gosaikunda basin, part of an area of many small lakes at high altitude. Because sources give different figures for the exact elevation of the lake, it is usually described simply as lying at high altitude in the Langtang National Park area rather than with a single stated height.

The lake is sacred to Hindus and is associated with Shiva, and it is the focus of an annual pilgrimage, particularly around Janai Purnima, when worshippers travel up to the lake. The wider basin contains a large number of small lakes and tarns, and the area was recognised as a Ramsar wetland site in 2007. The lake and its surroundings form part of the high country of the Langtang region, with alpine terrain, rocky slopes and seasonal snow above the tree line.

Visitors reach Gosaikunda on foot as part of a trek from the Langtang valley or from the ridge route to the south, staying at lodges in the settlements below the lake. The walking is over high ground, and the weather and snow cover determine when the route is passable. At the lake itself the setting is open and austere, and the place is as much a pilgrimage destination as a trekking objective.

destinations.name: Namo Buddha
destinations.short_description: A Buddhist pilgrimage site south-east of Kathmandu in Kavrepalanchok District, centred on a stupa and monastery in the hills.
destinations.description:
Namo Buddha is a Buddhist pilgrimage site in Namo Buddha Municipality, Kavrepalanchok District, Bagmati Province, in the hills south-east of Kathmandu, roughly 50 kilometres from the city by road. The site is centred on a stupa and a monastery standing on a ridge in the middle hills.

The place is associated with a well-known Buddhist story of the bodhisattva who gave his own body to feed a starving tigress and her cubs, and this account gives the site its religious importance. The stupa marks the place connected with that story, and the adjoining Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery is a large and active monastic complex that has grown around the pilgrimage site. Together they make Namo Buddha a living centre of Buddhist practice and teaching as well as a destination for visitors, and the ridge setting gives the site wide views over the surrounding hills.

Visitors generally reach Namo Buddha by road from Kathmandu or from the nearby town of Dhulikhel, arriving on the ridge above the monastery. The site is quiet and open, with the stupa, prayer flags and monastery buildings set among terraced fields and forested slopes. A visit can be brief or can include time at the monastery, and the route combines well with the hill country around Dhulikhel and Panauti.

destinations.name: Panch Pokhari
destinations.short_description: A group of five high alpine lakes in Sindhupalchok District, Bagmati Province, visited as a trekking and pilgrimage destination.
destinations.description:
Panch Pokhari is a group of five alpine lakes in Sindhupalchok District, Bagmati Province, north-east of Kathmandu. The name means five lakes, and the group lies in high country within the Langtang National Park area. The lakes sit far above the valley settlements, in open terrain that is snow-covered for part of the year. Because elevations given by different sources vary, the site is described here simply as high alpine rather than with a single stated height.

The lakes are a pilgrimage destination as well as a trekking objective, and they are visited in connection with local religious practice in the surrounding districts. The setting is one of alpine basins, ridges and small lakes rather than a single feature, and the route to them passes through forests and hill villages before reaching the high ground. The group is one of several high lake areas in the northern part of Bagmati Province, and its remoteness is part of what defines it.

Visitors reach Panch Pokhari on foot over several days, usually by a route that climbs from the lower valleys through settlements and forest to the lake basin. Accommodation is basic and generally takes the form of lodges or camping along the way. The walking is demanding because of the altitude and the length of the approach, and the accessible season is limited to the drier months when the high trails are clear of snow.

destinations.name: Chitwan National Park
destinations.short_description: Nepal's first national park, a UNESCO World Heritage site in the central Terai, known for rhinos, tigers, forests and Tharu culture.
destinations.description:
Chitwan National Park is a protected area in the southern central Terai of Nepal and was the country's first national park, established in 1973. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984. The property covers 93,200 hectares and extends over four districts: Chitwan, Nawalparasi, Parsa and Makwanpur. It ranges in elevation from about 100 m in the river valleys to 815 m in the Siwalik hills. Because it crosses districts and present-day provincial boundaries, it is not attributed to a single province.

The park is the last surviving major example of the natural ecosystems of the Terai, the lowland belt that once ran along the Himalayan foothills of Nepal and India. It lies between the Narayani (Gandaki) and Rapti rivers to the north and the Reu River and the Nepal-India border to the south, over the Sumeswar and Churia hills, and adjoins Parsa Wildlife Reserve to the east. Its mix of alluvial floodplain, riverine forest and grassland is prime habitat for the greater one-horned rhinoceros, which the park holds in one of the world's largest populations, and for the Bengal tiger. It is exceptionally rich in species, with over 350 bird species recorded, and it is also the land of the indigenous Tharu community, with Hindu pilgrimage sites such as Bikram Baba at Kasara and Balmiki Ashram at Tribeni.

Visitors come for wildlife in a lowland river setting. Jungle safaris by jeep or on foot, canoe trips on the rivers, birdwatching and visits to Tharu villages and cultural performances are the usual activities, and a buffer zone with community-run tourism surrounds the park. Beeshazar and its associated lakes within that buffer zone were designated a Ramsar wetland in 2003. Current park rules, seasons and entry arrangements should be checked before travel.

destinations.name: Beeshazar and Associated Lakes
destinations.short_description: An oxbow lake and wetland system in the Chitwan National Park buffer zone, listed as a Ramsar wetland site in 2003.
destinations.description:
Beeshazar and Associated Lakes is a wetland of oxbow lakes and surrounding water bodies in Chitwan District, Bagmati Province, in the Inner Terai of southern Nepal. It lies within the buffer zone of Chitwan National Park and was designated as a Ramsar wetland site of international importance in 2003, which recognises its value for waterbirds and wetland habitat.

The site takes its name from Beeshazar Tal, the main lake, and includes a group of associated lakes and pools set among forest and grassland in the flat terrain of the Inner Terai. The combination of open water, marsh, woodland and adjoining forest makes the area important for resident and migratory waterbirds and for other wetland wildlife, and its position inside the Chitwan buffer zone links it to the wider conservation landscape of the national park. The lakes also have local significance as a source of water and as part of the surroundings of the communities living near the buffer zone.

Visitors usually experience the area on foot or by bicycle along the tracks and embankments around the lakes, watching birds and looking for wildlife in the adjoining forest. The setting is quiet and flat, with open views across the water and through the surrounding trees, and the wetland is often visited alongside the national park. A visit is typically a half day of slow walking and observation rather than a set route.

destinations.name: Pokhara
destinations.short_description: A lakeside city in Kaski District and the capital of Gandaki Province, set against the Annapurna range and serving as the gateway to the Annapurna region.
destinations.description:
Pokhara is a metropolitan city in Kaski District and the capital of Gandaki Province in central Nepal. It stands at an average elevation of about 822 metres on the shore of Phewa Lake, roughly 200 kilometres west of Kathmandu, and the Annapurna range lies within a short aerial distance to the north. It is the second largest city in Nepal by population, with 600,051 residents recorded in the 2021 census, and it was formally declared the country's tourism capital in 2024.

The city sits where the middle hills meet the Himalayan foothills, and its setting is its defining feature: lake water in the foreground and snow-capped peaks, including Dhaulagiri, Annapurna I and Manaslu, on the horizon. Pokhara's history is tied to the old trade routes between India, Tibet and Kathmandu, and to the Kingdom of Kaski, of which it was a part in the 17th century. It is the main base for treks in the Annapurna Conservation Area and the Annapurna Circuit.

Visitors experience Pokhara as an unhurried base town with lakeside districts, viewpoints on the surrounding hills and easy access to the mountains. Typical activities include boating and walking along the lake, visiting the Tal Barahi temple on its island, hiking or driving up to hilltop viewpoints for the mountain panorama, and using the city as a starting point for longer treks. Caves, waterfalls and the lakeside tourist quarter are among the other stops commonly combined into a stay.

destinations.name: Phewa Lake
destinations.short_description: The largest lake in Gandaki Province, at Pokhara, with a temple on an island and mountain reflections, part of a Ramsar-listed lake cluster.
destinations.description:
Phewa Lake, also called Phewa Tal, is a freshwater lake in Kaski District, Gandaki Province, on the southern side of the Pokhara Valley. It lies at an altitude of about 742 metres and covers roughly 5.7 square kilometres, with an average depth of about 8.6 metres and a maximum depth of about 24 metres. It is the largest lake in Gandaki Province and one of the largest in Nepal, and it forms part of the Lake Cluster of Pokhara Valley, which was declared a Ramsar site in 2016.

The lake is the best-known feature of Pokhara and the centre of the city's lakeside life. The Annapurna range lies about 28 kilometres to the north, and the lake is known for reflections of Machhapuchhre and other peaks on its surface. Tal Barahi Temple, a two-storey pagoda dedicated to Vishnu, stands on an island in the middle of the water. The lake supports commercial fisheries and feeds a small hydropower plant at its outlet, and analysis of lake sediments indicates the basin formed in the late Pleistocene, over twelve thousand years ago.

The northern and eastern shores have developed into a visitor district of hotels, restaurants and shops, and the lake is used for boating and other water-based recreation. A typical visit involves taking a boat out to the island temple, walking the shoreline, and stopping at viewpoints for the mountain backdrop; the lake is also the reason many travellers choose Pokhara as a base before heading into the Annapurna region.

destinations.name: Annapurna Base Camp
destinations.short_description: A trekking destination in the Annapurna Sanctuary, a high glacial basin enclosed by peaks in the Annapurna Conservation Area north of Pokhara.
destinations.description:
Annapurna Base Camp sits in the Annapurna Sanctuary, a high glacial basin lying about 40 kilometres directly north of Pokhara in Kaski District, Gandaki Province. The sanctuary is an oval-shaped plateau at an altitude of over 4,000 metres, ringed by mountains of the Annapurna range, most of which exceed 7,000 metres. Its only entrance is a narrow valley between the peaks of Hiunchuli and Machapuchare, through which glacial run-off drains into the Modi Khola river. The whole area lies within the Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal's largest protected area at 7,629 square kilometres.

The sanctuary has long been significant to the Gurung people who live in the area, who regarded it as sacred, as the repository of treasures left by serpent deities and as the home of deities from Hindu, Buddhist and older animistic traditions. Local tradition once prohibited bringing eggs or meat into the sanctuary. The basin was not entered by outsiders until 1956, when Colonel Jimmy Roberts reached it while reconnoitring an approach to Machapuchare, and it was described as the Sanctuary in the book about that expedition. The terrain is dramatic in its contrast: south-facing slopes carry dense rhododendron and bamboo forest, while north-facing slopes lie in the rain shadow and are drier and colder.

Reaching base camp is a multi-day teahouse trek, typically approached from the Pokhara side via villages along the Modi Khola valley. The walk passes through farmland, forest and steep gorge country before emerging into the open basin, and much of the experience is the gradual change in vegetation, culture and temperature with altitude. Conservation-area rules restrict the number of outside travellers and the gathering of firewood and grazing of domestic animals.

destinations.name: Annapurna Circuit
destinations.short_description: A long-distance trekking route that encircles the Annapurna massif, crossing Thorong La pass and passing through Manang and Mustang.
destinations.description:
The Annapurna Circuit is a long-distance trek that encircles the Annapurna massif in the mountains of central Nepal. The route crosses two major river valleys and typically measures between about 160 and 230 kilometres, depending on where motor transport is used and where the trek is ended. Its highest point is Thorong La pass at 5,416 metres, on the edge of the Tibetan Plateau. The trail passes through Manang and Mustang districts and falls largely within the Annapurna Conservation Area.

The route's character comes from the range of country it crosses rather than a single highlight. It moves from subtropical paddy fields and forest at the lower elevations up through waterfalls, gorges and cliff country, past Hindu villages in the foothills and into the Tibetan-influenced culture of the Manang valley and lower Mustang. Mountain scenery at close quarters includes the Annapurna massif, Dhaulagiri, Machhapuchhre, Manaslu, Gangapurna and Tilicho Peak. The trek traditionally begins at Besisahar or Bhulbhule in the Marshyangdi valley and concludes in the Kali Gandaki gorge. Most trekkers walk it anticlockwise so that altitude is gained more gradually and the Thorong La crossing is easier and safer.

In practice the circuit is a multi-week teahouse trek, usually starting from Kathmandu with a stop in Pokhara. Much of the experience is village-to-village walking with river crossings on suspension bridges. Road construction has affected a large share of the original route and changed the villages along it, and marked side trails have been developed to avoid stretches of the new roads.

destinations.name: Muktinath Temple
destinations.short_description: A temple sacred to Hindus and Buddhists in Muktinath Valley, Mustang, known for its 108 water spouts and the natural flame of Jwala Mai.
destinations.description:
Muktinath is an ancient temple in Muktinath Valley in Mustang District, Gandaki Province, at the foot of the Thorong La mountain pass. It is a pilgrimage site sacred to both Hindus and Buddhists, who worship there as an abode of the Hindu deities Vishnu and Shakti and of the Buddhist bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara respectively. The temple stands in the high mountains of the Kali Gandaki region and is commonly described as one of the highest temples in the world.

The complex sits within a poplar woodland treated as a sacred grove, and it comprises several sanctuaries used by different traditions, including some rooted in older animistic worship. Its central shrine, built in Newar pagoda style with a three-tiered roof and a golden pinnacle, was constructed in its current form in the early 19th century, with the building dated to about 1814-1815. The courtyard is enclosed by 108 water spouts known as the Mukti Dharas, and the springs are understood to represent the 108 holy places of the Sri Vaishnava tradition. For Hindus the site is one of the Char Dham of Nepal and a place of liberation, while Tibetan Buddhists know it as Chumig Gyatsa, meaning Hundred Waters. The adjacent Jwala Mai temple is venerated for a sacred flame fed by natural gas emerging from the ground.

A visit to Muktinath means travelling into the dry, high landscape of lower Mustang, whether on foot as part of a longer trek in the Annapurna region or by road and short connecting flights to the Jomsom area. Many pilgrims move through the courtyard to pass beneath the 108 spouts, and the surrounding grove, ponds and subsidiary shrines are part of the same visit. Prayer flags, mountain views and the strong wind of the valley shape the experience of the site.

destinations.name: Tilicho Lake
destinations.short_description: A high glacial lake on the Annapurna circuit in Manang District, Gandaki Province, reached by a side trek through the Marsyangdi valley.
destinations.description:
Tilicho Lake is a glacial lake in Manang District, Gandaki Province, in the Annapurna range of the Himalayas. It lies within the Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal's largest protected area, and sits in high alpine terrain well above the tree line. Its elevation is reported differently by different sources, generally around 4,900 metres, and the lake is fed by glaciers and seasonal melt rather than by a large river system.

The lake is best known for its setting and for the unusual difficulty of reaching it. Because of the cold and the altitude, surveys have recorded no aquatic organisms in the lake itself, while the surrounding alpine zone supports hardy mountain wildlife. The lake also features in Hindu tradition, where it is associated with Kak Bhusundi of the Ramayana, and it drew attention in 2000 when a diving team carried out a high-altitude scuba dive in its waters.

Visitors reach Tilicho as a side trip from the Annapurna Circuit, usually leaving the main trail and walking up the Marsyangdi valley to a lodge settlement near the lake. The final approach crosses steep, exposed slopes and loose ground, so the route is normally done with a local guide and an acclimatisation stop. The reward is a stark, cold basin ringed by snow and rock, with wide views of the surrounding peaks.

destinations.name: Ghandruk
destinations.short_description: A traditional Gurung village in the Annapurna foothills of Kaski District, a common overnight stop on the Annapurna Base Camp trek.
destinations.description:
Ghandruk is a traditional Gurung village in Annapurna Rural Municipality, Kaski District, Gandaki Province. It lies in the foothills of the Annapurna range, roughly 32 km north-west of Pokhara, at an elevation reported at about 2,000 metres. Before the 2015 reorganisation of local government it was a separate village development committee; it now forms part of a larger rural municipality and is one of the larger surviving Gurung settlements in Nepal.

The village is known for its living culture as much as its position on the trail. Ghandruk is a Gurung community, and its stone-paved lanes, slate-roofed houses and neighbourhood temples reflect that heritage. It has a Gurung cultural museum and a long-established school serving the surrounding area. Local celebrations combine animist, Buddhist and Hindu practice, and the village is a common place to encounter Gurung music, dance and food rather than only passing through.

Ghandruk sits on the main Annapurna Base Camp trekking route and is also used as a base for walks toward Poon Hill. From the village and the ridges above it there are close views of Annapurna South, Machapuchare, Hiunchuli and Gangapurna. Visitors typically stay overnight in lodges or community homestays, walk the village lanes, visit the museum and temples, and continue the next day along the trail network.

destinations.name: Tsum Valley
destinations.short_description: A remote Buddhist valley in northern Gorkha District, inside the Manaslu Conservation Area and close to the Tibetan border.
destinations.description:
Tsum Valley is a remote Himalayan valley in the northern part of Gorkha District, Gandaki Province, close to the border with Tibet. It lies within the Manaslu Conservation Area, a protected area established in 1998 that covers a large part of the Mansiri Himal, and its settlements climb from roughly 1,900 metres to above 4,000 metres. The valley is reached mainly by following the Budhi Gandaki river corridor and is bounded by the Ganesh Himal, Sringi Himal and Boudha Himal ranges.

Tsum has strong cultural and religious ties to Tibet and is known among Tibetan Buddhists as a beyul, or hidden valley, understood as a place of spiritual refuge. Its inhabitants, the Tsumba, speak a Tibetan-derived dialect and maintain traditions that survived because the valley stayed largely closed to outsiders until the early 21st century. The valley holds important monasteries including Mu Gompa and Rachen Gompa, and the Tibetan saint Milarepa is believed to have meditated in caves here, making Tsum a place of pilgrimage. Subsistence farming and yak and sheep herding remain central to daily life.

Tsum is now walked as an extension of the Manaslu trekking route, with entry controlled as a restricted area, so trekkers travel with an organised group and the required permits. The walking is long and steep, passing mani walls, chortens and small villages, with high mountain scenery and a notably different cultural atmosphere from the main Manaslu trail. The valley was opened to trekkers in 2008 and now supports a modest flow of lodge-based trekking.

destinations.name: Bandipur
destinations.short_description: A preserved hilltop Newar trading town on the Mahabharat ridge in Tanahun District, Gandaki Province, known for its old main street and views.
destinations.description:
Bandipur is a hilltop settlement and rural municipality in Tanahun District, Gandaki Province. It sits on a saddle of the Mahabharat range at an elevation reported at roughly 1,030 metres, about 700 metres above the Marsyangdi River valley and between Kathmandu and Pokhara. The old town occupies a narrow ridge, with a single main street lined by two- and three-storey buildings whose back walls drop steeply down the hillside.

Bandipur was developed as a trade stop by Newar merchants from the Kathmandu valley after the region was conquered in 1768, chosen partly for its malaria-free height. It grew into a prosperous commercial centre on the India-Tibet trade route, and its Newar architecture, shuttered facades, slate-paved lanes and covered veranda along the main street survive largely intact. Its importance declined in the twentieth century after the Prithvi Highway was built in the valley below and the district headquarters moved to Damauli. Bandipur nonetheless retains a library, a large open Tundikhel and many historic houses.

Visitors come to Bandipur for the town itself and for the surrounding countryside. The car-free main street is best explored on foot, and the ridge offers wide views of the Marsyangdi valley and, on clear days, the Annapurna and Manaslu ranges. Walks lead to nearby Gurung and Magar villages, viewpoints and caves, and the town serves as a quiet base between Kathmandu, Pokhara and the Chitwan lowlands.

destinations.name: Manakamana Temple
destinations.short_description: A hilltop Hindu temple to the goddess Bhagwati in Gorkha District, Gandaki Province, reached by trail or by a long-running cable car.
destinations.description:
Manakamana Temple is a Hindu temple in Gorkha District, Gandaki Province, dedicated to the goddess Bhagwati. It stands on Kafakdada hill at an elevation reported at about 1,300 metres, above the confluence of the Trishuli and Marsyangdi rivers, roughly midway between Kathmandu and Pokhara. The name is commonly understood to mean the temple that grants the wishes of its devotees.

The temple is built in the pagoda style and is closely tied to the history of the Gorkha kingdom, from which the Shah rulers who unified Nepal emerged. Its legends connect it to a Gorkha queen and to the Magar priest Lakhan Thapa, and by tradition the priests of the shrine belong to his lineage. The temple has received patronage from Gorkha rulers over the centuries, and documents record donations of materials and worship provisions. It is one of the better-known pilgrimage sites in central Nepal and draws large numbers of devotees, particularly around major festivals.

Most visitors reach Manakamana either by walking up from the river valley or by taking the cable car that links Kurintar, in Chitwan, to the hill above the temple; the cable car began commercial operation in 1998 as Nepal's first such service. The temple compound includes the main shrine, an ambulatory and smaller shrines, and the hilltop opens to views of the surrounding valleys and, on clear days, the Annapurna and Manaslu ranges. The atmosphere is busiest on festival days and quieter on ordinary mornings.

destinations.name: Lumbini
alternate_names: Lumbini, the Birthplace of the Lord Buddha
destinations.short_description: The UNESCO-listed birthplace of the Buddha in Rupandehi District, Lumbini Province, with the Maya Devi Temple, Ashoka Pillar and monastic zone.
destinations.description:
Lumbini is a Buddhist pilgrimage site in Rupandehi District, Lumbini Province, in the Terai plains of southern Nepal. It is identified as the birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1997 under criteria (iii) and (vi). The inscribed property is small, about 1.95 hectares with a buffer zone of about 22.78 hectares, and is protected under Nepal's Ancient Monument Preservation Act. It is owned by the Government of Nepal and managed by the Lumbini Development Trust.

The archaeological conservation area contains the sacred garden, the Shakya Tank, the Maya Devi Temple and the sandstone Ashoka Pillar bearing a Pali inscription in Brahmi script. The Ashoka Pillar, erected in the third century BC, is the main documentary evidence for the site's identification. UNESCO describes excavated brick structures in a cross-wall system, Buddhist viharas from the third century BC to the fifth century AD and stupas from the third century BC to the fifteenth century AD, showing that Lumbini was an active pilgrimage centre over many centuries. The wider area also holds a master-planned monastic zone with temples and monasteries built by Buddhist communities from several countries, a museum and a research institute.

A visit to Lumbini centres on the peaceful sacred garden, the Maya Devi Temple and the pillar, with the surrounding monastic precincts and the museum explored on foot, by cycle rickshaw or by local transport. Many pilgrims come for meditation and devotion rather than sightseeing, and the flat Terai landscape, the sacred pond and the tree-lined paths give the site a quiet, contemplative character.

destinations.name: Maya Devi Temple
destinations.short_description: The main Buddhist temple at Lumbini, built over archaeological remains marking the traditional birthplace of the Buddha in Rupandehi District.
destinations.description:
Maya Devi Temple is the main Buddhist temple at Lumbini, in Rupandehi District, Lumbini Province. It stands inside the archaeological conservation area of the Lumbini World Heritage property, next to a sacred pool and within the sacred garden. The temple is named for Maya Devi, the mother of Siddhartha Gautama, and the site is traditionally identified as the place of the Buddha's birth.

Brick structures beneath and around the temple were formerly dated to the third century BC, the period of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, and the nearby Ashoka Pillar carries the inscription that identifies the site. Excavations reported in 2013 found the remains of an older timber shrine below the brickwork, pushing the sequence of worship here back to around the sixth century BC. The Maya Devi Temple area is therefore central to the archaeological case for Lumbini, alongside the excavated monasteries and stupas elsewhere in the property. The temple remains an active place of worship and pilgrimage rather than only a monument.

Pilgrims and visitors enter the temple to see the exposed archaeological remains and the marker associated with the birth, then walk the sacred garden and the pool beside it. The presentation is deliberately restrained, with the fragile brickwork protected and viewed from a walkway. Many visitors combine the temple with the Ashoka Pillar, the museum and the wider monastic zone, and the temple is busiest during Buddhist festivals and pilgrimage seasons.

destinations.name: Tilaurakot
destinations.short_description: An archaeological site in Kapilvastu District, on Nepal's UNESCO Tentative List as the remains of the ancient Shakya city of Kapilavastu.
destinations.description:
Tilaurakot is an archaeological site in Kapilvastu Municipality, Kapilvastu District, Lumbini Province, in the southern Terai. It lies about 25 km north-west of the Maya Devi Temple at Lumbini and is identified by Nepal's Department of Archaeology as the probable site of the ancient Shakyan capital, Kapilavastu, where the Buddha is said to have spent the first part of his life. It was submitted to Nepal's UNESCO Tentative List in 1996 as 'Tilaurakot, the archaeological remains of ancient Shakya Kingdom'; it is a tentative-list candidate, not an inscribed World Heritage property.

The site is among the better-preserved early historic city remains in South Asia. It consists of a fortified citadel of roughly 500 by 400 metres laid out on a regular grid, with an earthen and later brick wall that was built over an earlier wooden palisade. At its centre is a smaller walled complex with monumental gateways, and excavations have uncovered a stupa, tanks, industrial remains and a large quantity of iron slag radiocarbon-dated to around 400 BC. Finds at the site have been dated across a long sequence from early agricultural layers through Mauryan and later periods, and the city appears to have been planned from an early phase.

A visit to Tilaurakot is an archaeological and historical experience rather than a monument visit. The remains are low, grassy and spread across open ground, so interpretation depends on the excavation reports and on walking the outlines of the walls, gates and central complex. The site's identification with Kapilavastu has been debated by scholars, and visitors should treat the attribution as the leading but not universally accepted reading. The area sits within the wider Buddhist circuit around Lumbini and Kapilvastu, alongside sites such as Nigali Sagar.

destinations.name: Bardiya National Park
destinations.short_description: A large protected wilderness in Bardiya District, Lumbini Province, with Sal forest, grassland, the Karnali River and abundant wildlife.
destinations.description:
Bardiya National Park is a protected area in Bardiya District, Lumbini Province, in the western Terai of Nepal. It covers about 968 square kilometres, making it the largest and among the least disturbed national parks in Nepal's Terai, and it adjoins the eastern bank of the Karnali River, with the Babai River running through it. The park was first set aside as a hunting reserve in 1969, gazetted as a wildlife reserve in 1976 and upgraded to a national park in 1988, when it was known as Royal Bardia National Park. Its northern edge follows the crest of the Siwalik Hills.

The park's value lies in its range of habitats and the wildlife they support. About seventy percent of the area is forest, with the remainder a mix of grassland, savannah and riverine forest, and its flora and fauna inventories run to hundreds of species. The park is known for tigers, one-horned rhinoceros, Asian elephants, swamp deer and Gangetic dolphin in the Karnali, along with gharial and marsh mugger crocodiles and a long bird list that includes the Bengal florican and sarus crane. Together with the neighbouring Banke National Park it forms a large connected protected landscape that is important for tiger conservation.

Access is usually from Nepalgunj, from where the park headquarters at Thakurdwara is reached by road. Visitors stay in jungle lodges near the park boundary and explore on guided activities such as jungle walks, jeep drives, boat trips on the Karnali and river-side birdwatching. The regulated format suits a visit of several days, with mornings and late afternoons given to wildlife viewing and the middle of the day to rest. The dry months from autumn to spring are the most comfortable, while the pre-monsoon period is hot and the monsoon brings rain and restricted access.

destinations.name: Rani Mahal
destinations.short_description: A nineteenth-century Rana palace on the banks of the Kali Gandaki in Palpa District, Lumbini Province, since restored and opened as a museum.
destinations.description:
Rani Mahal, also called Ranighat Palace, is a historic Rana palace on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Palpa District, Lumbini Province. It was built in 1893 by General Khadga Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana, who had been exiled to the Palpa area after a failed attempt to remove the prime minister. The name means Queen's Palace: the building was raised in memory of his wife, Tej Kumari Devi, who died in 1892. It is not on the UNESCO World Heritage List, but the nearby medieval town of Tansen in the same district is on Nepal's Tentative List.

The palace is a product of its builder's position and resources. It was designed by a British architect and built over about four years with workers brought from India, a detachment of soldiers and local labour, and the surrounding forest and river ghats were renamed in the queen's memory. Khadga Shamsher abandoned Rani Mahal in 1902 when he left for India, after which the building stood without a caretaker and deteriorated through the twentieth century. The Government of Nepal funded a restoration completed in the 2010s, and a museum was established in the building. It is sometimes compared to the Taj Mahal because both were built in memory of a wife and stand beside a river.

The palace stands in a quiet riverside setting at the foot of forested hills, below Tansen. Visitors reach it by a short motorable road from Tansen or by a longer foot trail, and generally combine it with sightseeing in Tansen itself. The visit is largely an architectural and scenic one: walking the restored building, looking out over the Kali Gandaki, and taking in the wooded slopes and riverbank around the palace.

destinations.name: Tansen
destinations.short_description: A historic Newar hill town and the administrative centre of Palpa District, Lumbini Province, on Nepal's UNESCO Tentative List.
destinations.description:
Tansen is a municipality and the administrative centre of Palpa District, Lumbini Province, in the hills of central Nepal. It sits at an elevation reported at about 1,370 metres on the southern slope of Shreenagar hill, overlooking the Kali Gandaki valley, roughly between Butwal and Pokhara. The town was submitted to Nepal's UNESCO Tentative List in 2008 as 'The Medieval Town of Tansen' under criteria (iii), (iv) and (vi); it is a tentative-list candidate and has not been inscribed on the World Heritage List.

Tansen's history runs back to around the eleventh century, when the area formed part of the Bara Magarat, the twelve territories administered by Magar rulers. It later developed as a market centre for Newar traders and artisans known for metalwork and dhaka cloth, and it preserves a compact settlement of steep, narrow lanes lined with Newar shophouses, temples and monuments. Surviving structures include the Bhairab Temple, the Amar Narayan Temple, the Ran-Ujjeshwari Bhagawati Temple and the Tansen Durbar, the palace of the Rana governors, which was destroyed in 2005 and later rebuilt. Palpa was also the seat of the Sen kingdom that ruled the region for nearly three centuries.

Visitors experience Tansen on foot. The town centre is a walkable maze of alleys and small squares, and the walking is what reveals its architecture and street life. The surrounding hills offer viewpoints and short walks, and Tansen works well as a base for exploring Palpa District, including the nearby Rani Mahal on the Kali Gandaki. Its position on the highway between Butwal and Pokhara makes it a convenient stop between the Terai and the Annapurna region.
