destinations.name: Swargadwari
destinations.short_description: A hilltop Hindu pilgrimage site in Pyuthan District, Lumbini Province, associated with cows and the legacy of Swami Hamsananda.
destinations.description:
Swargadwari is a hilltop temple and pilgrimage site in Pyuthan District, Lumbini Province, in the mid-hills of western Nepal. It stands on a ridge above the surrounding valleys and is listed in Nepal's national inventory of cultural and historic heritage sites. The site is dedicated to Hindu worship with a special emphasis on the role of cows, and it is regarded as one of the better-known pilgrimage destinations in the country.

The temple is associated with Guru Maharaj Narayana Gautama Khatri, also known as Swami Hamsananda, who is said to have founded it and who spent much of his life in the area herding and milking large numbers of cattle. That pastoral tradition remains part of the site's identity, and resident cattle have long been kept at the temple complex. Over time the site developed into a religious centre with temples, ashrams and accommodation for pilgrims, and it has also been known for the donations of fodder and supplies that sustain its animals.

Pilgrims come to Swargadwari for darshan and for the quiet hilltop setting, walking or driving up to the temple complex and staying in its simple accommodation. The ridge gives wide views over the surrounding hills and the Dang and Pyuthan valleys. The site is busiest during major festivals and quieter on ordinary days, and a cable car connecting the base to the temple complex has been developed to improve access.

destinations.name: Ramagrama Stupa
destinations.short_description: A buried Buddhist relic stupa in Parasi District, Lumbini Province, on Nepal's UNESCO Tentative List as the relic stupa of the Buddha.
destinations.description:
Ramagrama Stupa is an ancient Buddhist stupa in Ramgram Municipality, Parasi District (Nawalparasi West), Lumbini Province, in the western Terai. It was submitted to Nepal's UNESCO Tentative List in 1996 as 'Ramagrama, the relic stupa of Lord Buddha' and is a tentative-list candidate, not an inscribed World Heritage property. UNESCO's entry describes it as the only undisturbed original stupa containing relics of the Buddha, and Nepal's Department of Archaeology dates its construction to between the Mauryan and Gupta periods.

According to Buddhist tradition, after the Buddha's death his remains were divided among eight kingdoms, each of which enshrined a portion in a stupa, with Ramagrama being the stupa of the Koliya kingdom. When the Mauryan emperor Ashoka later sought to collect the relics from these stupas to redistribute them, tradition holds that he was prevented at Ramagrama by a naga guarding the site, leaving it the one original stupa never opened. The reliquary is understood to remain in place. The mound is roughly 7 metres high with a complex measuring about 10 metres high and 23.5 metres in diameter, and the core has not been excavated. A geophysical survey detected a quadrangular Kushan-era monastery buried beneath the surface.

Because the stupa is unexcavated and covered by earth, a visit is quiet and low-key rather than monumental: visitors see the grassy mound and the surrounding site rather than exposed structures. The location is an active pilgrimage destination with a long history of veneration, and it sits within the wider Buddhist circuit of Lumbini Province along with Lumbini and Tilaurakot. Development and conservation planning for the site has been under way in recent years, with a masterplan for its conservation and enhancement presented in 2023.

destinations.name: Rara Lake
destinations.short_description: The largest freshwater lake in the Nepal Himalaya, set inside Rara National Park in Mugu District, Karnali Province, and listed as a Ramsar wetland.
destinations.description:
Rara Lake is a freshwater lake in Mugu District of Karnali Province, and the central feature of Rara National Park, which spans Mugu and Jumla districts. It is the largest lake in Nepal, with a water surface of about 10.8 square kilometres, a length of roughly 5 km and a maximum depth of 167 m, lying at about 2,990 m. The lake drains into the Mugu Karnali river system through the Nijar river, and it is covered by snow for part of the winter.

The lake is notable for its clear water, its changing colour through the day as light and weather shift, and the forested ridges that enclose it, including Chuchemara Danda at 4,087 m and Murma at 3,630 m. Rara snowtrout and a species of frog are recorded as endemic to the lake, and the surrounding park protects red panda, musk deer, Himalayan black bear, leopard and Himalayan tahr. It was included in Rara National Park when the park was established in 1976, and in September 2007 the lake and its surrounding wetland were designated a Ramsar site.

Visitors reach Rara on foot or by air; there is no road connection to the lake itself. A typical visit combines a trek through the park's coniferous and subalpine forest with time on the lakeshore, where boating, birdwatching and camping are the usual pastimes. The park headquarters and the lakeside settlement provide the main bases, and the weather is most settled outside the winter snows and the summer monsoon.

destinations.name: Rara National Park
destinations.short_description: Nepal's smallest national park, covering about 106 square kilometres of forest and alpine country in Mugu and Jumla districts around Rara Lake.
destinations.description:
Rara National Park is a national park in Karnali Province, spread across Mugu and Jumla districts. It was established in 1976 and covers about 106 square kilometres, making it the smallest of Nepal's national parks. Its elevation runs from roughly 2,800 m to 4,039 m at Chuchemara Peak, and Rara Lake, the largest lake in Nepal, sits at its centre.

The park protects temperate and subalpine forest of blue pine, rhododendron, spruce and juniper below about 3,200 m, shifting to fir, spruce and pine higher up. More than a thousand plant species have been recorded. It is known for a rich bird list of over 240 species, including wetland birds such as grebes, pochards and mergansers, and for mammals such as red panda, musk deer, Himalayan black bear, leopard, Himalayan tahr and the dhole. Rara Lake and its surrounding wetland were added to the Ramsar list in September 2007.

A visit is usually built around a trek, since the park has no road access to the lake. Trails from Jumla and the Talcha area approach the lake through forest and open ridge country, with camping and basic lodge accommodation along the way. Birdwatching, walking and time at the lakeshore are the main activities, and snow can close the higher routes in winter.

destinations.name: Shey Phoksundo National Park
destinations.short_description: Nepal's largest national park and its only trans-Himalayan one, covering Dolpa and Mugu districts in Karnali Province around Phoksundo Lake.
destinations.description:
Shey Phoksundo National Park lies in Karnali Province and extends across Dolpa and Mugu districts. It was established in 1984 and, at about 3,555 square kilometres, is the largest national park in Nepal and the only one that crosses the Himalayan range. Its land runs from roughly 2,130 m in the lower valleys to 6,885 m at the summit of Kanjiroba Himal, and its headquarters are at Palam in Dolpa. Phoksundo Lake, the park's best-known feature, lies in the upper Suligad valley.

The park spans a marked range of climates, from forested valleys in the south to the arid, high-altitude Dolpo plateau on the Tibetan side. Snow leopard, grey wolf, musk deer, bharal, argali, Himalayan tahr and Himalayan black bear are among the mammals recorded, and a survey carried out between 2019 and 2022 counted a significant snow leopard population. The park also contains several gompas, including Shey Gompa, and the Buddhist and Masto traditions of the Dolpo communities remain part of the landscape.

Reaching the park normally involves a flight to Dolpa followed by several days of walking, and camping is the standard form of accommodation. Treks typically combine the turquoise lake with high passes and the upper Dolpo plateau, and the park is used for both trekking and mountaineering. Weather and snow make the park a seasonal destination rather than a year-round one.

destinations.name: Phoksundo Lake
destinations.short_description: A deep turquoise alpine lake in Dolpa District inside Shey Phoksundo National Park, and a Ramsar wetland since September 2007.
destinations.description:
Phoksundo Lake is an alpine freshwater lake in Dolpa District, Karnali Province, and the central feature of Shey Phoksundo National Park. It sits at about 3,600 m in the upper Suligad valley and covers roughly 4.9 square kilometres. It is one of the deepest lakes in Nepal: a 2019 survey by the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology measured a maximum depth of about 136 m, following an earlier survey that found 145 m. In September 2007 the lake was designated a Ramsar site.

The lake is known for its strong blue colour and for the unusual setting of its southern shore, where the village of Ringmo stands on a large landslide dam that formed the lake. Below the dam the outflow drops away as a tall waterfall. The surrounding area is culturally Tibetan: more than twenty stupas stand in the northern belt, a gompa sits on the eastern side where annual prayers are held, and Buddhism and the Masto tradition are practised in lower Dolpo and Ringmo.

Phoksundo is normally reached on a trek from the Dolpa airstrip, walking up the Suligad valley over several days, with camping and simple lodges at Ringmo and along the route. Visitors come for the lake itself, the cliff and forest scenery around it, and the Bon and Buddhist sites nearby. Access is seasonal and depends on snow and trail conditions.

destinations.name: Sinja Valley
destinations.short_description: The ancient capital of the Khasa Kingdom in Jumla District, widely regarded as the birthplace of the Nepali language and listed on Nepal's UNESCO tentative list.
destinations.description:
Sinja Valley lies in Jumla District, Karnali Province. It was the capital of the Khasa, or Western Malla, kingdom, which held this part of the mid-western hills from roughly the 12th to the 14th century. The valley was added to Nepal's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list on 30 January 2008 in the cultural category, under reference 5263, on the basis of criteria concerning its cultural interchange and historical testimony.

Excavation work by the Department of Archaeology and Cambridge University uncovered the remains of palaces, temples and an old settlement, including a ring of large monolithic stone columns around the ruins, a Malla gateway and steps, and a network of earthen water pipes that points to an organised water supply. Caves across the Hima river hold Buddhist chaityas and cliff inscriptions. The valley is closely associated with the origin of the Nepali language and of the Devanagari script, with some of the earliest written examples found on local cliffs and at nearby Dullu. Masto shamanic rites are still practised at many of the stone temples, or dewal.

Sinja is reached on foot from the Jumla area and is generally visited as part of a trek through the surrounding valleys. The archaeological remains, the terraced farmland and the river setting form the shape of a visit, and the site is a stop for travellers interested in the region's Khasa-era history and in the deeper past of the Nepali language.
data_quality_notes: Historical interpretation, archaeological features and visitor access need confirmation from heritage authorities.

destinations.name: Kankre Bihar
destinations.short_description: A restored Shikhara Buddhist temple and archaeological site in Birendranagar, Surkhet District, associated with the medieval Khasa kingdom.
destinations.description:
Kankre Bihar, also spelled Kakre Bihar and Kakrebihar, is a Buddhist temple and archaeological site in Birendranagar, the district headquarters of Surkhet District in Karnali Province. It is a Shikhara-style temple, built in the 12th century according to published accounts, and it spreads over a large area of about 180 hectares. The temple was restored and reopened in September 2021. It is listed among Nepal's national heritage sites.

The site is understood to be the remains of an old Buddhist monastery and settlement and is connected with the wider Khasa kingdom culture of the region, alongside places such as Sinja and Dullu. Carved stonework, including Buddha-life scenes depicted in the temple sculpture, has been the subject of published study. Because the site is a standing monument in a provincial capital rather than a remote ruin, it can be visited without a trek.

Visitors reach Kankre Bihar directly in Birendranagar, a short distance from the town centre, and it is usually combined with other Surkhet sights such as Bulbule Lake and the town's viewpoints. The visit is a short walk around the restored temple, its stone carvings and the surrounding hilltop setting, making it a straightforward half-day stop for travellers passing through the Karnali lowlands.

destinations.name: Jumla
destinations.short_description: A historic hill town at around 2,500 m in Jumla District, Karnali Province, and a long-established trading and trekking gateway in the western hills.
destinations.description:
Jumla is a town in Jumla District, Karnali Province, and the centre of Chandannath Municipality. It lies at an elevation of about 2,500 m in the Tila valley, in the mid-western hills of Nepal. It is the district headquarters and the main service centre for the surrounding area, including routes towards Rara Lake and the districts to the north and west.

Jumla is known for its long history. The nearby Sinja Valley was the capital of the Khasa kingdom, and the wider district was an important part of that medieval polity. The town is also known for its distinctive red rice, marsi, which grows in the valley, and it is associated with a long tradition of trade routes linking the mid-western hills to the Terai and to the Tibetan plateau. The town itself is compact, with a bazaar around the temple area and a mix of Hindu and Buddhist cultural influences.

Visitors use Jumla as a gateway: it has an airfield and is a starting or finishing point for treks to Rara Lake and the surrounding valleys. The town offers basic accommodation and supplies, and the main things to do are walking the bazaar, visiting the temple, and using the town as a base before heading into the hills. Summers are mild and winters are cold, with snow possible.

destinations.name: Chandannath Temple
destinations.short_description: A Hindu temple in Khalanga Bazar, Jumla, dedicated to Dattatreya and the chief temple of the Jumla area in Karnali Province.
destinations.description:
Chandannath Temple is a Hindu temple in Jumla, in Chandannath Municipality of Jumla District, Karnali Province. It stands in Khalanga Bazar at an elevation of roughly 2,500 m. The temple is dedicated to Dattatreya, also known as Trimurti, and is the principal temple of the Jumla area.

Local tradition holds that a person named Chandannath came from Kashmir and brought the Dattatreya image, placing it where the temple now stands, and that construction followed under the Kallala, or Kalyal, dynasty. Few written records of the temple and that dynasty survive, and much of the account has been passed on orally. Chandannath is also credited in local belief with introducing marsi, the red or brown rice that Jumla is known for. A nearby Bhairabnath shrine stands alongside the temple, and the yearly lingo replacement ceremony is held at Ghatasthapana, the opening day of Dashain.

A visit to the temple is a simple town activity rather than a trek: it sits above the bazaar in Jumla and can be reached on foot from the town centre. Most visitors combine it with a walk through Khalanga Bazar and with the town's use as a base for treks towards Rara Lake and the Sinja Valley. The temple is an active place of worship, so visits are shaped by daily ritual and festival timing.

destinations.name: Khaptad National Park
destinations.short_description: A national park of about 225 square kilometres spread over four districts of Sudurpashchim Province, known for its grasslands, forests and religious sites.
destinations.description:
Khaptad National Park is a national park in Sudurpashchim Province. It was established in 1984 and covers about 225 square kilometres, extending across the four districts of Bajhang, Bajura, Achham and Doti. It ranges in elevation from about 1,400 m to 3,300 m. A buffer zone of about 216 square kilometres was declared in 2006. The park is associated with Khaptad Baba, a scholar and hermit who lived in the area and whose advice shaped its protection.

The park is a plateau of rolling grassland, steep slopes and streams, with forest of chir pine and rhododendron, oak, and Himalayan fir and hemlock. More than 500 floral species have been recorded, including a large number of medicinal plants. Mammals include leopard, Himalayan black bear, dhole and alpine musk deer, and a long bird list includes the Himalayan monal, peregrine falcon and white-rumped vulture. Within or beside the park are religious and cultural sites such as the ashram of Khaptad Baba, Khaptad Lake, Tribeni and the Ganesh temple, and the nearby Ramaroshan area of Achham has lakes and old building ruins.

A visit usually takes the form of a trek, since the park is remote and served by camping rather than hotels. Routes approach from Bajhang and from the Doti and Achham sides over several days, on trails through forest and open pasture. Walking, birdwatching and visits to the religious sites are the main activities, and the park is best visited in the spring and autumn seasons.

Park statistics here follow the standard reference figures (225 sq km; 1984; 1,400-3,300 m). NTB's page describes the highest point, Sahashra Linga, at 3,200 m, which is treated as a specific site rather than the park maximum.

destinations.name: Shuklaphanta National Park
destinations.short_description: A Terai national park of about 305 square kilometres in Kanchanpur District, Sudurpashchim Province, known for its grasslands and swamp deer.
destinations.description:
Shuklaphanta National Park is a protected area in the Terai of Sudurpashchim Province, in Kanchanpur District. It covers about 305 square kilometres of open grassland, forest, riverbed and wetland at an elevation of roughly 174 to 1,386 m, bounded by the Mahakali river on the west and south. The area was first declared a royal hunting reserve, then gazetted as a wildlife reserve in the 1970s, enlarged in the late 1980s, given a buffer zone in 2004, and finally changed to national park status in 2017.

The park contains Shukla Phanta, the largest continuous patch of grassland in Nepal, at around 16 square kilometres. It is best known for its herd of swamp deer, or barasingha, which is the largest known population of the species, and it also holds tiger, elephant, hog deer, chital and nilgai. Its bird list runs to several hundred species, including the Bengal florican, sarus crane and swamp francolin, and it is the western limit for several resident bird species. Mugger crocodile and other reptiles occur around the lakes, and the park forms part of the Terai Arc Landscape, with a corridor linking it to protected areas across the border in India.

Visits are usually made from the park headquarters area in Kanchanpur, reached by road or by a flight to Dhangadhi. Grassland and wetland areas such as Rani Tal are explored by vehicle and on foot with guides, and the main activities are wildlife viewing, birdwatching and jungle safaris. Lodges near the park provide accommodation, and the cooler months from autumn to spring are the most comfortable time to visit.

destinations.name: Api Nampa Conservation Area
destinations.short_description: A large conservation area of about 1,903 square kilometres in Darchula District, Sudurpashchim Province, centred on the Api and Nampa peaks.
destinations.description:
Api Nampa Conservation Area is a protected area in western Nepal, in Darchula District of Sudurpashchim Province. It was established in 2010 and covers about 1,903 square kilometres. Its elevation ranges from roughly 518 m up to 7,132 m at the Himalayan peak Api, and the area forms part of the Kailash Sacred Landscape. It is named after the two peaks Api and Nampa, and a grassland plateau sits at its centre, mixed with a range of forest types. It is a populated conservation area rather than an empty reserve, with tens of thousands of residents living in the villages within its boundary.

The conservation area was created to protect the biodiversity and cultural heritage of the upper Mahakali region. Snow leopard, musk deer, clouded leopard, goral, Himalayan black bear and Himalayan tahr occur here, along with birds such as the Himalayan monal, snowcock and blood pheasant. The area spans a strong altitude gradient, from subtropical valley country to permanent snow and ice, and it holds a mix of Hindu and Buddhist cultural traditions along the Nepal-India border zone.

Travel here is for trekking rather than sightseeing, and accommodation is mainly camping and village homestay-style lodging. Routes usually begin from the Darchula area and climb through forests and grazing grounds towards the Api and Nampa massifs, with the highest ground reserved for serious mountain travel. The district and access arrangements are remote, so conditions and permits should be checked with the conservation area office before planning a trip.

destinations.name: Badimalika Temple
destinations.short_description: A high-altitude Hindu Shakti Peeth temple in Triveni Municipality, Bajura District, Sudurpashchim Province, visited on foot during the monsoon festival.
destinations.description:
Badimalika Temple is a Hindu temple in Triveni Municipality, Bajura District, Sudurpashchim Province. It stands on a high ridge in the far-western hills, near the Budhi Ganga and Karnali rivers. The shrine is one of the major pilgrimage sites of Nepal and is regarded as a Shakti Peeth. It is dedicated to the goddess Bhagwati, also worshipped here as Malika Devi, and it is served by two priests, one representing Bajura district and one representing Kalikot district.

The temple is mentioned in the Skanda Purana and in the Swasthani Brata Katha. According to the Swasthani tradition, the shoulder of Sati fell at this place, and a temple was built where the body part came to rest. Its main festival is Malika Chaturdashi. Pilgrims come to the shrine seeking the fulfilment of wishes, and the surrounding high pastures and ridges are part of the pilgrimage setting.

Reaching Badimalika involves a trek through the far-western hills, typically over several days, with camping or basic local accommodation. The route is walked mainly as a pilgrimage rather than as a general sightseeing trip, and visitors combine the temple visit with the open grassland, or patan, country and mountain views along the way. Access is seasonal, and the area has been brought into a provincial forest conservation framework alongside nearby Ramaroshan.

destinations.name: Ghodaghodi Lake Area
destinations.short_description: A Ramsar-listed oxbow lake and wetland complex in Kailali District, Sudurpashchim Province, and a wildlife corridor between the Terai and the Siwalik hills.
destinations.description:
Ghodaghodi Lake Area is a wetland in Kailali District, Sudurpashchim Province, at an elevation of about 205 m on the lower slopes of the Siwalik hills. The Ramsar site covers about 25.6 square kilometres and was designated on 13 August 2003. The main feature is a shallow oxbow lake, with thirteen associated lakes and ponds, marshes, meadows and streams, and tropical deciduous forest on the surrounding slopes. Nepal Tourism Board describes the complex as a wildlife corridor between the lowland Terai and the Siwaliks.

The wetland is a religious and cultural site as well as an ecological one. It is a traditional festival venue for Tharu communities in the area, and it was declared Nepal's first bird sanctuary in March 2022. The lake and its surrounds support a large number of plant species and provide habitat for Eurasian otter, Bengal tiger and red-crowned roofed turtle, among others. Mugger crocodiles have been recorded across the lake complex, and the wetland is an important stop for resident and migratory water birds.

A visit to Ghodaghodi is a lowland excursion rather than a trek. The lakes and forest can be explored on foot along the shore and the surrounding trails, and the area is used for birdwatching, nature walks and cultural visits during festival periods. It lies near the Mahendra Highway in Kailali District and is normally visited as a half-day or day trip from the surrounding towns.
